豬膀胱提琴原為歐洲與美洲民間樂器，早期由流浪樂師與乞丐使用至十九世紀初。其前身是: The bladder fiddle was originally a folk instrument of Europe and the Americas, used by travelling musicians and beggars into the early nineteenth century. Its forerunner was a bowed instrument of the musical-bow kind, a long stick with gut strings and an inflated pig's bladder, which later developed one to three strings in Poland, Lithuania, the Netherlands and elsewhere. By 1675 the Dutch had replaced the bladder with a drum hoop, forming the bumbass; immigrants carried it to the Pennsylvania German community in the United States, where it became percussion instruments such as the boomba. German troops in the First World War also used tin cans as resonators. Today it divides into bowed types such as Lithuania's pūslinė and the percussion type used in Europe, North America and Australia.

The percussion type strikes with a stick and bounces the instrument on the ground to shake bells, cymbals and blocks, and can come close to a drum roll and other percussion sounds; if tuned strings are kept, drawing the notched stick across them gives a rough sound, and when a spring replaces the string today it is purely percussion. The bladder fiddle is a folk chordophone popular in Europe and the Americas, H-S 321.321-7. It is basically a long stick, one or more thick gut strings and a pig's-bladder resonator, played with a notched wooden stick or a horsehair bow; it was played early on by travelling musicians and beggars and was still found in folk music into the early nineteenth century, and can be either serious or comic. Today it divides into bowed and percussion types: the bowed type survives in Lithuania and elsewhere, and in the folk music of Europe, North America and Australia it developed into a percussion instrument struck, bounced and shaken with attached bells and cymbals.
